The best test for evaluating your interactions with prospective employers is this: “Would this be appropriate to convey in a condolence or get-well card?” Obviously, you wouldn’t use emoticons or web shorthand (lol; fwiw; u; numbers where words belong) when offering condolences. Don’t use any informal or lazy constructs when writing in a professional context.

The bottom line? Proactively sending a note like this (rather than ignoring their attempts to contact you) will ensure you remain in their good graces if a position you like is available in the future with the recruiter and/or employer.

You can withdraw a LinkedIn job application in three main ways depending on how you applied: directly through LinkedIn (“Apply” via Easy Apply or LinkedIn Jobs), via the employer’s external application system, or by contacting the recruiter/hiring manager. Steps and tips below.

When you applied through LinkedIn (Easy Apply or Apply on LinkedIn)

- Open LinkedIn and go to Jobs (top menu).
- Click “My Jobs” (or “Applied” / “Manage applications”).
- Find the job and click it to open the application details.
- If the platform supports withdrawal, you will see a “Withdraw application” or “Withdraw” button — click it and confirm.
- LinkedIn records the withdrawal; the employer sees that the applicant withdrew.
Notes:

- “Withdraw” is not always available. If no withdraw button appears, the employer may have closed applications or requires direct contact.
- Withdrawn applications are typically recorded but retained in LinkedIn history; you can reapply later unless the employer disallows it.
When the job redirects to an external site (employer ATS)

- In My Jobs, open that application — LinkedIn will show a link to the external application site.
- Click the link, sign in to the employer’s portal (you may need an account), and look for a withdraw/cancel application option in that ATS.
- If no withdraw option exists, use the portal’s contact or help function to request withdrawal.
When neither LinkedIn nor the ATS offers withdrawal, or you want to be explicit

- Locate the recruiter or hiring contact:
- Check the job posting for recruiter/contact details.
- Look at the company page and job poster profile.
- Use messages in LinkedIn (InMail) if you previously corresponded.
- Send a short, professional message or email:
- State your name, job title applied for, application date, and that you’d like to withdraw your application.
- Example: “Hello [Name], I applied for [Job Title] on [date]. Please consider this message as a withdrawal of my application. Thank you for your time.”
- Keep a copy of the message for records.
Practical tips and considerations

- Timing matters: withdraw promptly if you no longer want to be considered; late withdrawals may already be in review.
- If you accepted an interview elsewhere or have a conflict, politely withdrawing preserves your professional reputation.
- If you might reapply later, mention that briefly when contacting the recruiter (optional).
- If you want to hide applications rather than withdraw, LinkedIn doesn’t offer a private “hide” — only withdrawal or leaving it in your history.
- For privacy or data concerns, consult the employer’s privacy policy or LinkedIn’s help center for how application data is stored and deleted.
If you encounter technical issues

- Clear browser cache or try a different browser/device.
- Use LinkedIn Help Center -> Contact Us to report a missing withdraw option.
- If an external ATS blocks withdrawal, ask the employer’s HR team to remove your application.
This covers the practical methods to cancel or withdraw a LinkedIn job application and how to proceed when LinkedIn or the employer’s system does not provide a direct withdraw button.

💡 Did you know? You can withdraw or remove a job application on LinkedIn if you changed your mind or applied by mistake!
Even if it was through an external website👍
✅ Why it matters 👉 It helps you keep your job search organized, professional, and focused on the right opportunities.
😅لا تقلق، كلنا ضغطنا "تقديم" بالغلط مرة في حياتنا - لكن لكل مشكلة حل 👌

HOW TO ⁉️
1. Withdraw Your Application
Some job postings have a “Withdraw” button. Steps:
Go to Jobs → My Jobs.
Find the job you applied for.
If available, click Withdraw application.
Confirm your withdrawal.
This option is not available for all postings, especially if the employer uses external application links.
2. Contact the Employer Directly
If you cannot withdraw via LinkedIn:
Find the contact email for HR or the recruiter.
Politely explain that you’d like to withdraw your application.
❇️ Example:
“Dear [Name], I recently submitted my application for [Job Title] but would like to withdraw it. Thank you for your understanding.”
3. Delete Draft Applications (for LinkedIn Easy Apply)
If you started but didn’t submit via Easy Apply, you can delete the draft from My Jobs → Applied.
Once submitted, deletion is not possible; you can only withdraw.

99% of jobs posted on LinkedIn are fake.

That’s what a lot of frustrated job seekers say.
And they’re wrong.

Here’s what most people don’t understand about how LinkedIn hiring actually works:

When a recruiter posts a free job on LinkedIn, they only receive 25 applications.
That’s it.

Once those 25 applications are reached:
→ The job automatically stops accepting applications
→ Or the recruiter has to pay to keep it open

Whenever you see more than 25 applications on any job, that means it is a paid job post.
And LinkedIn is not cheap.

In fact, LinkedIn job postings are significantly more expensive than platforms like Naukri or Indeed.

So ask yourself this:
Why would a company spend thousands just to post “fake” jobs?

They wouldn’t.

What’s actually happening is this:

→ You’re applying late
→ The application limit is already full
→ The role is still open internally but closed externally
→ Or the recruiter is sourcing candidates directly instead of reviewing new applications

And then it feels like the job was fake.

The real problem isn’t fake jobs.

The real problem is how people apply.

If you’re only:
→ Mass applying
→ Applying after 2–3 days
→ Relying only on the “Apply” button

You’re already behind.

What works better:
→ Applying early
→ Reaching out to recruiters or hiring managers
→ Having a resume and LinkedIn profile that actually converts

LinkedIn isn’t broken.
Your strategy probably is.

And fixing that changes everything.

A job search hack that very few people use, but it can genuinely change how you apply.

If you are serious about targeting a company, do this one step before sending your resume.

Steps are:
1. Open LinkedIn search.
2. Use the filter called “People who worked at this company”.
3. Now look for profiles that left in the past one or two years and are still active on LinkedIn.
These are the people you want to speak with.

>> Send them a simple, respectful message like this:
“I am planning to apply to your previous company. If you are open to a short chat, I would love to understand what skills or experiences they value most. I am happy to compensate for your time.”

They will tell you things that HR and job descriptions will never mention.

Entering the job market can be challenging, but there are strategies to enhance your chances of success. Here are some key points to consider when working with recruiters:

Top 8 worst takes I saw on LinkedIn in 2025 (for job seekers):
“Don’t use Open to Work.”
Visibility helps. Shame doesn’t.

“Apply ASAP or you’ll miss out.”
Speed ≠ fit. Relevance wins.

“ATS rejects 75% of resumes automatically.”
Pure myth. Panic marketing at its finest.

“If ATS doesn’t rank you first, no human will see it.”
Humans, filters, and search still exist.

“Only apply if you tick every requirement.”
JDs are wish lists, not checklists.

“Your resume must be one page. Always.”
Context > arbitrary rules.

“Rejected once = blacklisted forever.”
Wrong. Rejections are role-specific, not permanent records.

“Just network more.”
Lazy advice without the who, how, or why.

⚠️ Bad advice spreads because it’s simple and confident.
💡 Good advice takes nuance, context, and empathy.
👉 Job searching is already tough. Don’t let myths make it harder.
👉 If advice makes you feel ashamed, invisible, or broken—challenge it first.

Job searching should be about possibility, not panic. The truth is- #visibility , #relevance , and #humanconnection matter far more than myths or rigid rules.

Let’s spread advice that empowers, not discourages.

Because every job seeker deserves to feel seen, capable, and hopeful about the opportunities ahead.
